query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multicomponent bcc high-entropy alloys, substituting a portion of the conventional d‐electron elements with an actinide (or lanthanide) element introduces delocalized f‐electron states that hybridize with the conduction band, thereby modifying the electron–phonon coupling and controlling the superconducting transition temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional superconducting HEA (e.g., [TaNb]1-x(TiZrHf)x) with established superconductivity (Tc in the 3–8 K range) and a homogeneous bcc solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Partially substitute one of the d‐electron elements (such as Ti or Zr) with an actinide element (e.g., U) at a level that maintains a total of at least five elements (each above 5 at%) in the solid solution.
generation.conditions: Samples must be synthesized under identical processing conditions (ensuring a homogeneous bcc solid solution with no phase separation) and measured under controlled pressure and temperature environments to isolate the effect of the f‐electron substitution.
generation.structural_mediator: Delocalized f‐electron states provided by the introduced actinide element and their interaction with the d‐electron conduction band.
generation.mechanism: The f‐electron states from the actinide element hybridize with the conduction electrons, thereby altering the density of states at the Fermi level and modifying the electron–phonon coupling strength. This in turn adjusts Tc relative to a baseline HEA composed solely of conventional transition metals.
generation.predicted_outcome: The actinide-containing HEA is predicted to exhibit a measurable shift in Tc compared to the conventional HEA. Depending on the balance between enhanced electron–phonon coupling and any potential scattering or magnetic pair-breaking effects, Tc may either increase or decrease by an amount that is significant beyond experimental error. The direction and magnitude of this shift remain somewhat uncertain.
generation.baseline: The superconducting state of a d‐electron-only HEA (e.g., [TaNb]1-x(TiZrHf)x) with a Tc typically between 3 and 8 K and known robust superconductivity under standard conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold within single-phase, fully disordered bcc HEAs synthesized under conditions that preserve the solid solution. Deviations such as the onset of magnetic ordering or phase separation could lead to a breakdown of the assumed mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the net effect of the f‐electron inclusion will enhance or suppress Tc overall. The competing roles of increased electron–phonon coupling versus potential scattering or magnetic pair-breaking due to f‐electron localization are not fully quantified at this stage.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two series of HEA samples: one series will be the conventional d‐electron HEA (e.g., [TaNb]1-x(TiZrHf)x) serving as the baseline, and the second series will have an identical overall composition except that a fixed fraction of a conventional element is replaced by an actinide element (e.g., U). Ensure both series are processed under identical conditions to form homogeneous bcc solid solutions.
measurements: Determine Tc via electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements.
Perform specific heat measurements to probe changes in the density of states at the Fermi level.
Use XRD to confirm phase homogeneity and structure.
Examine microstructure via electron microscopy to verify a uniform elemental distribution.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant and reproducible change in Tc or related electronic properties (indicative of altered electron–phonon coupling) is observed between the actinide-containing HEAs and the baseline series, then the hypothesis that f‐electron hybridization governs superconducting behavior in HEAs is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Most studies have focused on combinations of transition metal elements to produce HEAs, but it is interesting to ask whether lanthanide or actinide elements can be introduced as well. This would have several advantages with both practical and basic science implications. For instance, f-electron elements such Ce, Yb, U, Np, Pu, and Am exhibit valence flexibility, have a tendency to hybridize with conduction electrons and have large spin anisotropy. Other examples such as Nd, Sm, Gd-Tm, and Cm-Cf feature well localized f-states with associated magnetism. These characteristics often lead to novel properties that include unconventional magnetic order, complex electronic order, topologically protected states, structural instabilities, and superconductivity. Indeed, recent studies of HEAs that are composed entirely of lanthanide elements show that they exhibit complex magnetism with evidence for spin-glass behavior. It was also recently shown that the presence of a high entropy alloy-type blocking in the series REO0.5F0.5BiS2 enhances the superconductivity of this system. Actinide based alloys are also of interest for development of solid solutions (i) that form under extreme conditions,

[TaNb]0.31(TiUHf)0.69 thus emerges as an example of a small but growing family of f-electron materials with both practical and fundamental implications. Earlier work revealed that the Zr-based analogues and other HEAs exhibit high strength, ductility, and damage resistant properties across a broad range of temperatures, and the work presented here demonstrates that this extends to the actinide family. This suggests that this and other HEAs may provide a next generation waste form for radioactive isotopes, similar to other HEA systems. We also anticipate that the [TaNb]1-x(TiAHf)x HEA series will accommodate other radioactive elements (A = actinide) in the place of A = U. This has the advantage that it will enable studies of the direct impact of natural radiation damage and the long term robustness of these materials. It is also appealing to consider that variation of the stoichiometry may improve the superconducting properties and the introduction of other actinide or even lanthanide elements may induce novel behavior that might include magnetism, as has already been observed for other f-element HEAs.
